summary: Details the SONET/SDH technology-specific information needed when sending Link Management Protocol test messages. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a router can treat several physical links as one traffic engineering link, it has to check that the links are really connected. This document says how the Link Management Protocol does that over SONET and SDH optical links, and adds messages that let one router ask its neighbour to watch the trace bytes in the optical overhead and report a mismatch.

subtitle: How Link Management Protocol test and trace messages ride over SONET and SDH optical links.

tldr.problem: The Link Management Protocol checks that traffic engineering links are really connected, using test messages. On SONET and SDH links the protocol needs to know which part of the optical overhead to use and how to check the trace bytes that already travel in that overhead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SONET and SDH values for the Verify Transport Mechanism bit mask, including the J0, J1 and J2 trace correlation mechanisms, and adds a set of trace monitoring messages so one node can ask its neighbour to watch a link for a given trace pattern and report a mismatch.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from October 2005 and was later updated by RFC 6898. It registers eleven new LMP message types and two new object classes.

facts.label: New error codes
facts.value: 0x01 unsupported trace type, 0x02 invalid trace message

today: RFC 4207 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It was later updated by RFC 6898; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: LMP and Why SONET/SDH Needs Its Own Encoding
sections.content:
For scalability purposes, multiple physical resources that interconnect Label Switching Routers can be combined to form a single traffic engineering link for path computation and signaling. These resources may represent one or more physical links that connect the routers, or they may represent a Label Switched Path if LSP hierarchy is used. The management of traffic engineering links is not restricted to in-band messaging and can be done with out-of-band techniques.

The Link Management Protocol, defined in RFC 4204 as part of the Generalized MPLS protocol suite, manages these links. It consists of four main procedures, the first two mandatory and the last two optional. Control channel management establishes and maintains control channel connectivity between adjacent nodes, using a Config message exchange followed by a lightweight keep-alive message exchange. Link property correlation aggregates multiple data links into a single traffic engineering link and synchronizes the link properties. Link verification verifies the physical connectivity of the data links and exchanges their Interface_Ids. Fault management is primarily used to suppress alarms and to localize failures in both opaque and transparent networks. When LMP is used with SONET or SDH, the fault management procedures may not be needed, since existing SONET and SDH mechanisms can be used.

This document defines the SONET and SDH technology-specific information for LMP: the test procedures used for link verification and link property correlation, including the trace correlation transport mechanism defined for the J0, J1 and J2 bytes, which supports a separation of the transport and control plane identifiers. The trace correlation procedure requires a new trace monitoring function, which the document also discusses.
sections.plainLanguage: The Link Management Protocol groups several physical links into one logical link and checks that they are really connected. This document covers the optical detail: where in the SONET and SDH overhead the check messages go.

sections.title: Link Verification
sections.content:
In RFC 4204 a link verification procedure is defined in which test messages are transmitted in-band over the data links. It is used for data plane discovery, for exchanging Interface_Ids, which are used in Generalized MPLS signaling either as port labels or as component link identifiers depending on the configuration, and for physical connectivity verification. Multiple data links can be verified using a single verification procedure, and the correlation is done with the Verify_Id assigned to the procedure.

As part of the procedure, a BeginVerify message exchange is used to agree on the parameters for the test. It can be initiated by sending a BeginVerify message over the control channel, and it includes a BEGIN_VERIFY object with fields that specify, among other things, the transmission bit rate, the encoding type and the transport mechanisms for the test messages. If the remote node receives a BeginVerify message and is ready to begin, it sends a BeginVerifyAck message specifying the desired transport mechanism for the test messages, and it also assigns a Verify_Id to the procedure and includes it in the acknowledgement.

The transmission rate of the data link over which the test messages will be sent is represented in IEEE floating-point format using a 32-bit number field and expressed in bytes per second. The encoding type identifies the encoding supported by an interface and is consistent with the LSP Encoding Type of RFC 3471; for SONET and SDH it must equal the value given for SDH ITU-T G.707 and SONET ANSI T1.105. The transport mechanism is defined with the Verify Transport Mechanism bit mask, whose scope is restricted to the link encoding type. Multiple bits may be set in a BeginVerify message, but only one bit may be set in a BeginVerifyAck message.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the test starts, the two routers agree on how fast the link is, which encoding it uses and how the test messages will be carried. The reply from the far end picks one transport mechanism and carries a number, the Verify_Id, that ties the test to those links.

sections.title: Verify Transport Mechanism Values
sections.content:
The Verify Transport Mechanism field is 16 bits in length, and all values are defined in network byte order. The RFC defines the flags for SONET and SDH encoding. The value 0x0001 is reserved. The value 0x0002, named DCCS, means a test message over the Section or Regenerator Section data communications channel, capable of transmitting test messages using the DCC Section or RS Overhead bytes with bit-oriented High-Level Data Link Control framing; the test message is sent as defined in RFC 4204. The value 0x0004, named DCCL, means a test message over the Line or Multiplex Section data communications channel, using the DCC Line or MS Overhead bytes with the same HDLC-like framing.

The value 0x0008, named J0-trace, is capable of transmitting the SONET or SDH Section or RS trace over the J0 Section or RS overhead byte. The test message is not transmitted using the J0 bytes, that is, not over the data link, but is sent over the control channel and correlated for consistency to the received J0 pattern. To map the Interface_Id over which the J0 test message is sent to the J0 pattern sent in-band, the transmitting node must provide the correlation between the pattern and the J0 test message, done with the TRACE object.

The value 0x0010 and 0x0020 are reserved. The value 0x0040, named J1-trace, is the Path trace correlation over the J1 Path overhead byte for STS SPE or HOVC, and the value 0x0080, named J2-trace, is the Path trace correlation over the J2 Path overhead byte for VT SPE or LOVC. Both work the same way as J0-trace: the test message travels on the control channel and is correlated to the pattern received in band, with the TRACE object providing the mapping. The test message format in all three trace cases is a common header, a LOCAL_INTERFACE_ID, a VERIFY_ID and a TRACE object.
sections.plainLanguage: The transport mechanism is a 16-bit mask. Two values send the test message in a data communications channel in the optical overhead. Three values, for the J0, J1 and J2 trace bytes, send it on the control channel instead and compare it against the pattern already travelling in the overhead.

sections.title: Trace Monitoring
sections.content:
The trace monitoring features let a node watch the overhead of a link using the SONET and SDH capabilities. A node may request its neighbour, the remote node, to monitor a link for a specific pattern in the overhead, using the TraceMonitor message; an example of such an overhead is the SONET Section Trace message transmitted in the J0 byte. If the actual trace message does not match the expected trace message, the remote node MUST report the mismatch condition. A node may also request the value of the current trace message on a given data link with the TraceReq message, and a node may request a remote node to send a specific trace message over a data link with the InsertTrace message.

The TraceMonitor message, message type 21, is sent over the control channel and is used to request that the remote node monitor a data link for a specific trace value, which is inserted in the TRACE object. Its format is a common header, a MESSAGE_ID, a LOCAL_INTERFACE_ID and a TRACE. The remote node MUST respond with either a TraceMonitorAck or a TraceMonitorNack message. The TraceMonitorAck, message type 22, acknowledges receipt and indicates that all the TRACE objects were received and processed correctly, meaning there was no trace mismatch. The TraceMonitorNack, message type 23, acknowledges receipt and indicates that the TRACE object was not processed correctly, either because the trace monitoring requested is not supported or because there was an error in the object values.

The TraceMismatch message, message type 24, is sent over the control channel to report a trace mismatch on a data link for which trace monitoring was requested. Its format is a common header, a MESSAGE_ID and one or more LOCAL_INTERFACE_ID objects, and the LOCAL_INTERFACE_ID is the local Interface Id of the data link that has a trace mismatch. A neighbouring node that receives a TraceMismatch message MUST respond with a TraceMismatchAck, message type 25. The TraceReq message, type 26, requests the current trace value of a data link and carries a TRACE_REQ object; the TraceReport message, type 27, is sent in reply and MUST include a TRACE object for the requested data link. A TraceReqNack, type 28, is sent instead when the request cannot be honoured, and it MUST include an ERROR_CODE object. The InsertTrace message, type 29, asks a remote node to send a specific trace message over a data link, assuming the remote knows the mapping between the local and remote Interface_Ids; the remote node MUST respond with an InsertTraceAck, type 30, or an InsertTraceNack, type 31, and once the acknowledgement is received the TraceMismatch message is used to report a mismatch.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new request and report pairs let the two ends of a link keep an eye on the trace bytes. One asks the neighbour to watch for a pattern and report a mismatch, one asks what the current trace value is, and one asks the neighbour to put a particular trace value onto the link.

sections.title: The TRACE Object
sections.content:
The TRACE object has class number 21 and C-Type 1, Trace. Its layout is a flags byte with the N bit, a C-Type field, a Class field of 21 and a Length field, followed by a 16-bit Trace Type, a 16-bit Trace Length and the trace message itself. The Trace Type is the type of the trace message, and the RFC defines six values, with all other values reserved: 1 is SONET Section Trace in the J0 byte, 2 is SONET Path Trace in the J1 byte, 3 is SONET Path Trace in the J2 byte, 4 is SDH Section Trace in the J0 byte, 5 is SDH Path Trace in the J1 byte and 6 is SDH Path Trace in the J2 byte.

The Trace Length is the length in bytes of the trace message, as specified by the Trace Type. The trace message is the value of the expected message to be received in-band, and the valid length and value combinations are determined by the specific technology. The message MUST be padded with zeros to a 32-bit boundary if necessary, and the Trace Length does not include those padding zeroes. This object is nonnegotiable, which means a receiver that cannot understand it must reject the message rather than ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: The TRACE object carries the expected trace pattern, how long it is, and which of the six SONET or SDH trace bytes it belongs to. The pattern is padded to a four-byte boundary, and the length field does not count that padding.

sections.title: Error Codes and Trace Mismatch
sections.content:
The ERROR_CODE class uses a new C-Type, number 3, called TRACE_ERROR, and defines two new error code bit values: 0x01 means Unsupported Trace Type and 0x02 means Invalid Trace Message. All other values are reserved, and multiple bits may be set to indicate multiple errors. This object is nonnegotiable.

If the Trace type is not supported, the ERROR_CODE MUST indicate "Unsupported Trace Type". If the TRACE object was not equal to the value seen in the trace, the TraceMonitorNack message MUST include the ERROR_CODE indicating "Invalid Trace Message", and the TraceMismatch message SHOULD NOT be sent as a result of the mismatch. The TraceMonitorNack and the other negative acknowledgements use this same new ERROR_CODE C-Type, and the ERROR_CODE object carries an error for the requested data link.
sections.plainLanguage: Two error codes are added: one says the kind of trace byte is not supported, the other says the pattern found was not the one expected. A receiver that cannot handle these cannot ignore them, so it has to reject the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: LMP message security uses IPsec as described in RFC 4204. This document introduces no other new security considerations beyond those covered in that earlier specification. The trace monitoring messages inherit the protection that the Link Management Protocol already applies to its control channel exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: These messages travel under the same protection as the rest of the Link Management Protocol, which uses IPsec. The document adds nothing new on security.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The Link Management Protocol defines four name spaces in which IANA can make assignments: LMP Message Type, LMP Object Class, LMP Object Class type, which is unique within the object class, and LMP Sub-object Class type, also unique within the object class. This memo introduces new assignments in the first two of these.

Eleven message types are registered: TraceMonitor as message type 21, TraceMonitorAck as 22, TraceMonitorNack as 23, TraceMismatch as 24, TraceMismatchAck as 25, TraceReq as 26, TraceReport as 27, TraceReqNack as 28, InsertTrace as 29, InsertTraceAck as 30 and InsertTraceNack as 31. Two object classes are registered, TRACE with class name 21 and C-Type 1, and TRACE REQ with class name 22 and C-Type 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo asks IANA to reserve eleven message numbers for the new trace messages and two object class numbers for the objects they carry.

messages.label: TRACEMONITOR
messages.note: Asks the neighbour to watch a data link for a given trace value.

messages.label: TRACEMONITORACK
messages.note: Confirms the request was processed with no mismatch.

messages.label: TRACEMISMATCH
messages.note: Reports that the trace seen on the link did not match the expected value.
